ch00.note: Xuantong (宣統) was the reign title of Puyi, the last emperor of the Qing dynasty, who came to the throne as a small child in 1908. Its second year corresponds to 1910 and its third to 1911; the dynasty fell in the revolution of 1911–1912, so these are the closing years of imperial China. The novel pairs each reign–year with its Western date, as here.

ch01.note: Bannermen (旗人) were members of the Eight Banners, the hereditary military and social organization of the Manchu Qing dynasty. To call the Rong family Bannermen marks them as part of the ruling Manchu caste—a caste that, in this year of 1911, stood on the very eve of the dynasty’s fall.

Jinlian (金莲) means ‘golden lotus,’ the conventional term for a woman’s bound foot. The name is pointed: this bride has natural, unbound feet (天足), and Master Rong prides himself on opposing foot-binding—so she is a ‘golden lotus’ that was never bound. The lotus embroidered on the muddied shoe in the Prologue belongs to the same motif.

ch01.anchor: withered like a yellow leaf in the west wind
ch01.note: The chapter title, 草木摇落露为霜 (‘grass and trees shed their leaves, and dew turns to frost’), is a line from the Yan ge xing (燕歌行, ‘Song of Yan’) by Cao Pi (187–226), long taken as the earliest complete seven-syllable-line poem in Chinese: the autumn wind is bleak, the weather cold; grass and trees shed their leaves, and dew turns to frost. Its images of autumn decline set the key for a chapter of deaths, a lost child, and a withered wife.

ch02.note: Historically accurate. The Manifesto of the Communist Party was first published in London in February 1848; the 1888 English edition mentioned just below—translated by Samuel Moore and edited by Engels—is likewise real. The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen to which Cong Feng compares it was adopted in 1789, during the French Revolution.

Lin Daiyu—and the other names in this passage: Jia Tanchun, Xue Baochai, Shi Xiangyun, Qingwen, Siqi, Xiren, Yuanyang—are all figures in the eighteenth-century novel Dream of the Red Chamber (红楼梦). Lishui flatters herself with the young ladies’ sensitivity, talent, shrewdness and grace; A-Chu privately assigns her the maidservants’ sharp tongues and pride instead. The whole comparison is lost on a reader who does not know the book.

The chapter title, 朝生春晖暮留霭 (‘born at dawn to spring’s light, wrapped in mist by dusk’), turns on 春晖, ‘spring sunlight’—a classical figure for a mother’s love, from Meng Jiao’s (751–814) Youzi yin (游子吟, ‘Song of the Wandering Son’), which asks how the heart of an inch-long blade of grass can ever repay the light of three spring months. It is Fourth Madam’s maternal hold, not the abstract authority of the Rong house, that binds the wandering A-Chu.

ch03.anchor: sunk in the pond to drown
ch03.note: Chen tang (沉塘), ‘sinking in the pond,’ was a lineage punishment in old rural China: an offender against sexual morality—an adulterer, or a couple who eloped—might be bound and drowned in a village pond on the clan’s authority. Rong Sheng invokes it to measure how far England lies from home.

The source here reads 威尔逊卡迪芙 (‘Wilson Cardiff’). Cardiff is the capital of Wales (威尔士), and 威尔逊 (Wilson) appears to be a slip in the source for 威尔士; it is rendered simply as Cardiff throughout, as elsewhere in the book.

The chapter title, 同林春鸟各自飞 (‘birds of the same wood each take flight’), invokes the folk saying husband and wife are birds of the same wood; when calamity comes, each flies its own way (夫妻本是同林鸟，大难临头各自飞). The chapter scatters its pairs: A-Chu turns back from Cong Hui to save a stranger’s child, and Cong Hui reaches the harbour only to find him already gone.

ch04.note: Juntong (军统) is shorthand for the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Nationalist Military Affairs Commission, the Kuomintang’s secret-police and intelligence service. Strictly, it bore that name only from 1938; in 1931 its institutional forebears were just taking shape, so the term is used a little anachronistically here. The Communist Special Branch (特科) on the other side, however, was real and active in Shanghai from 1927, which fits the novel’s date exactly.

The two codenames are drawn from classical nature-images. Piaofeng (飘风, ‘whirlwind, drifting wind’) echoes the Daodejing: a whirlwind does not last a whole morning. Shiyu (时雨, ‘timely rain’) is the seasonable rain of the classics, falling just when it is needed. Wind and rain, the storm about to break, run all through this chapter’s talk of ‘a storm tonight.’

The chapter title, 阴差阳错难提防 (‘by a cross-grained twist of fate, hard to guard against’), rests on the idiom 阴差阳错—literally a ‘yin-error, yang-mistake,’ a chain of small chances that throws everything awry. The chapter runs on such accidents: a lost admission notice, a stranger’s helping hand, and a crate that proves to be nothing like what it seems.

ch05.note: The chapter title, 时人不识凌云木 (‘the people of the day know not the cloud-piercing tree’), and the couplet Du Luning recites are from the quatrain Xiao song (小松, ‘The Little Pine’) by the late-Tang poet Du Xunhe (杜荀鹤, 846–904): from small a prickly seedling deep in the grass, and now little by little it clears the weeds; the people of the day know not the cloud-piercing tree, till it has pierced the cloud, and then they call it high. Long read as the poet’s self-portrait, it turns on the failure to recognize greatness before it is obvious—exactly Du Luning’s point about the untried Yang Muci. Where the received text reads 直待 (‘wait until’), the novel quotes 直到 (‘until’).

ch05.anchor: Is it not a joy to learn
ch05.note: Du Luning opens with the first lines of the Analects of Confucius (论语 1.1): Is it not a joy to learn and to practice in season what one has learned? Is it not a delight to have friends come from afar? Is he not a gentleman who feels no rancor though others take no note of him? The ‘Sayings of Master Zeng’ he quotes a moment later—each day I examine myself on three points—are Analects 1.4, the words of Confucius’s disciple Zengzi (曾子). That a spymaster should recast the Confucian program of self-cultivation as a lesson in obscurity and infiltration is the passage’s deliberate irony.

‘Director Dai’ is Dai Li (戴笠, 1897–1946), head of the Nationalists’ military-intelligence apparatus and one of the most feared men in Republican China, sometimes called ‘China’s Himmler.’ His formal command of the Juntong dates only from its founding in 1938; naming him here, in a scene set in 1931, is of a piece with the novel’s slightly early use of ‘Juntong’ (see the note at Chapter 4).

ch06.note: Gege (格格) was a Manchu title borne by daughters of the Qing imperial house and higher nobility, roughly ‘princess’ or ‘young lady of rank.’ To nickname He Yashan ‘He Gege’ is to mark her, half in earnest and half in mockery, as a scion of the fallen Qing aristocracy—the ‘old Qing loyalists and their heirs’ (清朝遗老遗少) of the sentence before.

‘Save the children’ (救救孩子) is the famous closing cry of Lu Xun’s A Madman’s Diary (狂人日记, 1918), the founding story of modern Chinese fiction, where it is the diarist’s last hope that a generation not yet made cannibal might still be spared. In He Yashan’s mouth the words carry that literary charge—a plea against a devouring world—beneath their plain surface.

The chapter title, 宫花旋落已成尘 (‘the palace blossom, swiftly fallen, is already dust’), draws on the ‘palace flower’ (宫花) of Tang verse—the blossom in the deserted palace that stands for youth and beauty spent unseen, as in Yuan Zhen’s Xing gong (行宫): lonely, the old traveling-palace; its palace flowers red in silence. The exact line does not appear to be a quotation from any single canonical poem; it works rather as an echo of that whole tradition, bodied out here in the two young lovers cut down and in the fainting girl Rong Sheng sees fall like a flower.

‘The judge of horses had met his thousand-li steed’ renders 伯乐总算遇到了千里马: Bole (伯乐) was the legendary judge of horses of antiquity, and a ‘thousand-li horse’ (千里马) one that could run a thousand li in a day—together a byword for a discerning patron who recognizes rare talent, Du Luning casting himself as Bole to Yang Muci’s steed. In the digital source a stray line of pirate-website advertising (‘阳光中文网 www.sunshe.com…’) is appended to this sentence; it belongs to the file, not the novel, and is kept verbatim in the bilingual record but left out of the reading text.

ch07.note: The chapter title, 却疑春色在邻家 (‘and I half-suspect the spring’s colors are next door’), is the closing line of Yu qing (雨晴, ‘Clearing After Rain’) by the late-Tang poet Wang Jia (王驾): before the rain, first the buds seen among the flowers; after the rain, not a flower left beneath the leaves; the bees and butterflies in a throng go over the wall—and I half-suspect the spring’s colors are next door. Its wistfulness—beauty always just elsewhere, just out of reach—keys a chapter of longings deflected and a homecoming that rings a little hollow. (The widely printed ‘蜂蝶纷纷…却疑’ wording is the version polished by Wang Anshi.)

‘The Old Buddha’ (老佛爷) was the customary honorific for the Empress Dowager Cixi (慈禧, 1835–1908), who dominated the late-Qing court for nearly half a century. Fourth Madam’s unfinished boast—that she once attended the Old Buddha—places her, before her life in the Rong house, among the palace women of the last imperial reigns.

ch07.anchor: the pearls had returned to Hepu
ch07.note: ‘The pearls had returned to Hepu’ renders the idiom 合浦珠还. Hepu (合浦), a southern coastal commandery famous in Han times for its pearl fisheries, was said to have lost its oysters when grasping officials over-harvested them, and to have seen them return only when an upright governor, Meng Chang, restored good rule (Book of the Later Han). Ever since, the phrase has meant the recovery of something precious once lost—here, First Madam’s son restored to her.
